subject: physics
question_text: a) State Newton’s second law of motion. Hence derive F = ma from it. b) A body is moving along a circular path such that its speed always remains constant. Should there be a force acting on the body?

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 5 LONG ANSWER 1 — the only 8-mark form the book prints for this unit, and the TSBIE Basic Learning Material prints no Section C for Laws of Motion at all. The 2+3+1+2 split across the two parts is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher; no exam appearance years are printed, so appearances[] stays empty.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: a) The statement

lines.text: a) Newton’s second law of motion:

lines: The rate of change of momentum of a
body is directly proportional to the
external force applied on it, and takes
place in the direction of that force.
steps.margin_note: Both halves earn marks — the proportionality AND the direction. Do not stop after the first.
steps.why: The law is stated in momentum, not in acceleration. F = ma is a consequence of it, which is exactly what part (a) asks you to show.
common_mistakes: Stating the law as "F = ma", which is the thing you are being asked to derive.
Leaving out "in the direction of the force".

recall.must_convey: That the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and is in the direction of that force.
accept: rate of change of momentum is proportional to the force
and it acts in the direction of the force
momentum change rate force ki proportional
reject: F equals k times dp by dt

steps.memory_tip: State the law in MOMENTUM: rate of change of momentum, in the direction of the force. F = ma comes later.

steps.label: Write it in symbols
lines: Let a force F act on a body of mass m.
By the statement above,
where k is a constant of proportionality.
steps.margin_note: Introduce k here and say what it is. It has to be dealt with before the derivation can end.
steps.why: A proportionality cannot be used for calculation. Turning it into an equation is what k is for, and disposing of k is the last step.
common_mistakes: Writing F = dp/dt straight away, skipping the constant and losing the step.

recall.must_convey: That the proportionality is written as F = k dp/dt with a constant k.
accept: F is proportional to dp by dt
F equals k times dp by dt
k is the constant of proportionality
k ane constant pedatam
reject: rate of change of momentum is proportional to the force

steps.memory_tip: Proportionality first: F ∝ dp/dt. Then insert k to make it an equation.

steps.label: Put p = m v
lines: Momentum p = m v, and the mass of the
body is constant, so
steps.margin_note: State that m is constant before taking it outside. That is the assumption the step rests on.
steps.why: Only a constant mass may be pulled out of the derivative. For a rocket, whose mass changes, this line would not be allowed.
common_mistakes: Taking m out of the derivative without saying it is constant.

recall.must_convey: That p = m v is substituted and m, being constant, comes out of the derivative.
accept: p equals m v so substitute it
mass is constant so it comes out
F equals k m dv by dt
mass constant kabatti bayataki vastundi
reject: dv by dt is the acceleration

steps.memory_tip: You may pull m out of d(mv)/dt only because m is constant — write that line.

steps.label: a) The result
lines: But dv/dt is the acceleration a, so
In SI units the unit of force is chosen
so that k = 1. Therefore
steps.margin_note: Say WHY k = 1 — it is a choice of unit, not a piece of algebra.
steps.why: One newton is DEFINED as the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². That definition is what makes k exactly one.
common_mistakes: Setting k = 1 with no reason given.

recall.must_convey: That dv/dt is the acceleration and k = 1 in SI units, giving F = ma.
accept: dv by dt is the acceleration
in SI units k is one
so F equals m a
SI units lo k equals one
reject: p equals m v so substitute it

steps.memory_tip: k becomes 1 by the definition of the newton: 1 N gives 1 kg exactly 1 m/s².

steps.label: b) The circular path
steps.margin_note: One circle, the body, the tangential v and the force to the centre. Four strokes carry the whole of part (b).
steps.why: The picture shows the two directions that matter: velocity along the tangent, force towards the centre — permanently at right angles.
common_mistakes: Drawing the velocity along the radius instead of along the tangent.

recall.must_convey: That a circular path is drawn with the velocity along the tangent and the force towards the centre.
accept: draw the circle with v tangent and F to the centre
circular path figure
circle geesi tangent lo v force centre ki
reject: the direction of the velocity changes

steps.memory_tip: Draw the circle with two arrows: velocity along the tangent, force toward the centre.

steps.label: b) The answer

lines.text: b) Yes, a force must act on the body.

lines: On a circular path the DIRECTION of the
velocity changes at every point, even
though the speed does not. A changing
velocity means the body is accelerating,
and an acceleration needs a force.
steps.margin_note: Answer yes first, then give the reason. The reason is the direction change, not the speed.
steps.why: Velocity is a vector, so it changes when its direction changes even if its size is fixed. Constant SPEED is not constant velocity.
common_mistakes: Answering "no, because the speed is constant" — the commonest error in this chapter.

recall.must_convey: That yes, a force acts, because the direction of the velocity keeps changing so the body accelerates.
accept: yes a force is needed
direction of velocity changes so it accelerates
speed is constant but velocity is not
velocity direction marutundi kabatti force kavali

steps.memory_tip: Constant speed is not constant velocity — the direction changes, so there is acceleration, so there is a force.

steps.label: The name and formula
lines: This acceleration points to the centre.
It is the centripetal acceleration, and
the force causing it is

lines.text: F = m v² / r, towards the centre.

lines: For a stone whirled on a string, the
tension in the string supplies it.
steps.margin_note: Unmarked in this split, but it names the force and costs two lines. Write it if there is time.
steps.why: Naming the force and giving its size turns a qualitative "yes" into a complete answer, and it is the same idea the next chapter builds on.
common_mistakes: Calling it centrifugal force. That is not a real force on the body.

recall.must_convey: That the force is named centripetal and F = mv²/r is given.
accept: it is called centripetal force
F equals m v squared by r
centripetal acceleration towards the centre
centripetal force ani antaru

steps.memory_tip: Name it: centripetal force, F = mv²/r, pointing to the centre.

insider_note: Part b) is 3 of the 8 marks. Answer it as its own question, with its own figure.
